The line opens with a C3 clef and a three-sharp key signature. Next come five notes at one pitch (E4), beamed as eighths, with the first and last shorter. They match the end of bar 70: E4 16th, E4 8th, E4 8th, E4 8th, E4 16th. So the line begins partway through bar 70, which the previous line started. A barline follows.

The next bar is bar 71. It has four groups of four 32nds: a lower group (E4), two higher groups (A4 ×8) and a slightly lower group (F#4 ×4). Then one long beamed run of 16 high 32nds is written out. That run is the two B4 quarter tremolos in 32nds, so the bar is complete. A barline follows.

The last bar is bar 72. It has four groups of four 32nds, all at one low pitch (E4). That is the first half of the bar. The line ends with a wavy sign, most likely a custos (a mark pointing to the next line's first note). The bar's second half (the two E4 quarter tremolos) must be on the next line. So the line ends partway through bar 72.

Nothing contradicts the edition. The copyist writes the tremolos out as 32nds instead of using the edition's tremolo shorthand.
insights: The line was easy to match. The five repeated eighth-length notes before the first barline only fit the end of bar 70. Bar 71's E–A–F#–B pattern of 32nds, then the all-E bar, pins the rest. The hard parts were the written-out tremolos and the half-finished last bar with its wavy end sign. The next line's opening, or a clearer view of the end sign, would confirm that bar 72 carries over.
